notes: The whole-body acrobatic pose was judged successful, so the failure is localized rather than evidence against action-pose capability. User technical teaching clarified that a normal human/person render should structurally account for four fingers and one thumb per hand before finish; occlusion may hide a digit but must not terminate its construction. The user also distinguished anatomical completeness from functional hand semantics: a grasp-like hand must have a mechanically coherent thumb/finger/contact configuration. No corrective rerender, isolation test, retention test, or transfer test has yet been performed.
observations: The extreme acrobatic pose, foreshortening, silhouette, and overall action read successfully.

The prominent front/right hand failed digit integrity: the little finger began to render, became occluded by the ring finger, and then visually terminated instead of remaining structurally accounted for.

The rear/left hand lacked a clearly resolved thumb, contained incompletely rendered fingers, and suggested a grasp-like action whose spread digits did not describe a coherent grip or contact relationship.
Both visible hands therefore failed independently even though the global figure action succeeded.

notes: The user requested three separate images of ten hands each; the produced artifact was one composite sheet with three rows of ten. That delivery-format miss does not invalidate the sheet as an isolation test of hand execution. User review ultimately scored 22 of 30 hands acceptable after a second-pass correction. A supplied human hand photograph clarified only the broader need to validate whole-hand mechanical attainability; it is not evidence that one exact finger arrangement should be canonized as universally impossible. No retention or transfer retest has yet been performed.
observations: Twenty-two of thirty isolated varied-action hands were accepted; eight contained identifiable anatomical, biomechanical, or rendering defects.

Top-row #4 had incomplete or ambiguous digit count and thumb identity; middle-row #7 read as three long fingers plus two thumb-like branches, showing that five protrusions alone do not satisfy normal hand anatomy.
Top-row #7 began an index-finger chain that then visually terminated or fused into the palm instead of remaining structurally continuous.
Middle-row #8 and bottom-row #4 failed at the whole-hand configuration level: the individual digit forms did not combine into a convincing mechanically attainable hand pose.
Bottom-row #2 had a displaced or dislocated-looking thumb root/orientation.
Bottom-row #3 used a shadow/value mark that created a false apparent bend in an otherwise simple raised finger.
Bottom-row #8 omitted a useful thumbnail/orientation landmark, leaving an otherwise good thumb under-resolved at finish.
The remaining twenty-two hands demonstrated acceptable pointing, open-hand, fist, grip, support, object-contact, and gestural solutions in the same isolation run.
task: Generate thirty isolated human hands across varied positions and actions, including pointing, grabbing, grasping, holding, and related gestures, as a hand-practice drill

notes: This event records the corrected grip sheet after the user rejected an earlier same-view grip sheet and required varied front, side, three-quarter, and foreshortened viewpoints. The user judged 26 of 30 studies passable. Three were definite failures and one additional secondary hand was under-resolved but not counted as a definite failure. Because rigid objects constrain palm orientation and finger wrap, this run suggests object geometry can scaffold hand construction, but it did not eliminate digit-count errors. The run occurred after the first hand-canon intervention; memory consultation remains unproven.
observations: Twenty-six of thirty varied-angle grip studies were judged passable across guns, blades, poles, tools, and other rigid or semi-rigid objects.
Middle-row #14 substituted an object/handlebar-like form where the hand instance should have been, a task-instance presence failure rather than an anatomical hand failure.
Middle-row #16 contained a secondary/bottom gripping hand with only three long fingers resolved.
Middle-row #18 contained one thumb plus five long fingers, a clear extra-digit topology failure.
#21 had a good front hand but an under-resolved string-pulling secondary hand; the user withheld a strong critique because that hand was not fully rendered.
The broad success across multiple viewpoints indicates that front, side, three-quarter, and foreshortened grip views did not by themselves cause widespread anatomical collapse.

notes: The user requested a second no-object isolation test with random hand actions, varied angles, and foreshortening. User review identified seven failures and judged 23 of 30 passable. Follow-up technical teaching proposed a preventative construction route: establish the expected character-specific hand topology first, map the digit roots, fully construct the most obscured required digit before progressively nearer digits, count completed chains against the expected topology, and reject hidden construction only after overlap is solved. The user also cautioned against universalizing the human 4+1 topology: established character/species anatomy and references must override the provisional humanlike fallback. This teaching informed a reviewed canon refinement after the event; it is not evidence that the refinement has transferred yet.
observations: Twenty-three of thirty no-object hand studies were judged passable across varied front, side, three-quarter, folded, open, pointing, fist, and foreshortened views.

#1 folded the ring and little fingers unnaturally into the palm; the ring-finger attachment became separated and the buried distal/nail structure disappeared, although the little-finger bend itself was comparatively plausible.

#4 contained a hidden true thumb behind a thumb-like digit that should have been a finger, an unattached middle-finger structure, and additional downstream fingers; the finished silhouette concealed a broken root topology.

#5 had an index finger curled toward the palm without a convincing finger-side palm-wedge attachment near the middle finger, while the thumb sat too far forward and did not attach coherently to the thenar mass.
#12 contained an extra digit concealed by overlap/shadow: a low curled form plus another fingertip emerging behind the index/middle group.
#24 contained five long fingers plus one thumb, a six-digit hand.
#29 treated the thumb too much like another long finger, with weak root/opposition identity.
#30 failed closed-fist mechanics: the curled fingers did not form a convincing coupled closure and the thumb followed an implausible downward/outward path rather than participating coherently.
The error pattern concentrated on digit topology/root attachment, extra digit chains, and thumb identity rather than on viewpoint variety itself.

notes: Teacher confirmed that all four compositions were excellent. The controlled-comparison failure was slight ruin/environment drift between thumbnails, not weak composition. Future same-scene angle studies must lock the concept/environment identity first and vary only camera position, framing, scale, foreshortening, and visibility.
task: Compare one fixed scene across camera-angle thumbnails

notes: Teacher confirmed that the accepted thumbnail establishes the composition foundation for every later stage. Stage 1 through Stage 4 must preserve the prior stage's camera, framing, major masses, placement, negative spaces, and scene identity while allowing minor cleanup and clarification. Onion-skinning makes continuity visible; minor drift is tolerable, but redesign breaks the staged construction. Broken Gate succeeds because its continuity remains strong even though it is not perfect.
task: Maintain composition continuity from thumbnail through successive drawing stages

notes: Teacher judged the moth-and-teacup thumbnails excellent and continuity stable, but camera exploration was too narrow: most views came from the same right-side family, two were near-identical, and one pair differed mainly by close-up versus long shot. Effective camera search must vary lateral side as well as height, distance, tilt, and framing; scale changes alone do not constitute a meaningfully different camera.
task: Compare one fixed scene across genuinely different camera angles

notes: Teacher confirmed that the expressive change came from the pencil mark language and value treatment, not from changing the underlying scene design.
observations: The same locked scene design and camera family remained useful when the medium changed from marker to graphite pencil.
Pencil hatching, edge softness, line direction, and value emphasis made the thumbnails expressive in a different way without redesigning the camera or scene identity.
Distinct camera views still produced distinct narrative possibilities while the concept stayed continuous.
task: Compare one fixed scene across pencil-only camera thumbnails

notes: Teacher clarified that the pencil and marker sets should be judged primarily as small thumbnails rather than enlarged images.
observations: A thumbnail is meant to capture the essence of a possible image, not present a finished render.
Reduced-size review is the meaningful test: composition, silhouette, value grouping, focal point, and story should survive when detail disappears.
A 600x900 pixel target at 300 DPI, equivalent to a 2x3 inch thumbnail, is a useful practical scale; exact raster dimensions matter less than small-view readability.
task: Review thumbnails at their intended reduced viewing size
